title: A Fake Reference, a Phantom Statistic, but No Retraction
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Stephen Vainker continues his long-running investigation into education researcher John Hattie, documenting a lengthy correction issued by the journal Frontiers in Education after Vainker flagged a fake reference, a phantom statistic, and multiple misattributed citations in one of Hattie's papers. Rather than retract the paper as COPE guidelines on AI misrepresentation would suggest, the journal issued an extensive correction instead, which Vainker argues does not go far enough given further contradictions he found in the paper's ethics statement and methods section. He frames the episode as symptomatic of a broader failure in educational academia to police research integrity, suggesting that Hattie's legal team may be discouraging institutions from taking stronger action. The piece situates this single case within Vainker's wider argument that academic institutions are protecting influential but fraudulent scholarship because of the prestige and funding it brings. Ultimately, Vainker argues the stakes are institutional trust itself: if journals will not retract clearly AI-generated, fabricated scholarship, the public's ability to trust educational research erodes.
points: Frontiers in Education issued a correction rather than a retraction despite finding a fake reference and a fabricated statistic in Hattie's paper, even though COPE guidelines list undisclosed AI involvement as retraction-worthy.

Vainker identifies a direct contradiction between the paper's ethics statement (no informed consent required) and its methods section (claiming adherence to informed-consent guidelines), which he attributes to AI-generated text the authors did not review.

The piece argues that legal intimidation from Hattie's law firm may be discouraging Melbourne University, the publisher Elgar, and Frontiers from taking stronger action against a well-documented pattern of plagiarism and data recklessness.
Vainker frames the case as a test of whether academic institutions will protect their own integrity-checking mechanisms or continue shielding high-prestige, high-revenue scholars from accountability.
quotes: Academia, and especially education academia, is under the spotlight for its questionable rigour and integrity.
There will always be fraudulent and low quality research being produced - it does little good to wag our fingers at it.
It is likely that his use of the Elit law firm is also playing a major role.
More than likely, AI wrote the methods section and so the authors were unaware of the contradiction they were forming.
For academia to continue to have a prominent role within society, it is imperative that the public can, on the whole, trust the knowledge that it produces.
Disreputable researchers can forge careers, while universities and institutions may turn a blind eye to academics and students who bring in prestige and money to the university.
If it is not removed, and if the rest of Hattie's plagiarised and AI-authored work is not removed, then there is little hope for the forces safeguarding academic integrity to win out.
